To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) squarks and sleptons can have nonuniversality at the LHC; (b) the trilepton final states can be especially useful for studying this nonuniversality; (c) the nonuniversal spectrum can be distinguished from the universal one, with a universal scalar and a universal gaugino mass at the GUT scale, in the trilepton channel.

(i) the LHC can distinguish between nonuniversal and universal scalar mass spectra; (ii) the trilepton final state is the best for this purpose; and (iii) the dilepton and jet final states are also very good.

, in the context of the above scenarios, the trileptons are more sensitive to the scalar mass spectrum than are the like-sign dileptons and that the trilepton signal can have a sizable contribution from squark-gluino and gluino-quark decays, as well as from the direct decays of squarks and gluinos.

The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of the trileptons and the dilepton channels, it would be hard to differentiate between a minimal supergravity model and a model with nonuniversality.

, in the case of a nonuniversal spectrum, the LHC will have the ability to differentiate between different models of supersymmetry breaking, even if they have similar values for the lightest Higgs mass.
